title: By the river Chebar (Ezekiel 1)
hook: among exiles in Babylon, a vision of a chariot of fire and wheels

segments.voice: Yesterday, a king cut Jeremiah's scroll into the fire, and the prophet and Baruch wrote it all again, with more. Your line was there were added besides unto them many like words. What did you put back on paper? Today, a new prophet, far from home. Day eight hundred nine.
screen: `THERE WERE ADDED BESIDES UNTO THEM MANY LIKE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Where does God live? For many in Judah, the answer had an address: Jerusalem, the Temple, the holy of holies. Now some of them have been carried off to Babylon. They sit by the river Chebar, a long way from that address. Among them is Ezekiel, whom the text calls a priest, far from the Temple where priests serve. And the book of Ezekiel opens there, with his own words, in the King James Bible: "as I was among the captives by the river of Chebar, that the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God." Not in Jerusalem. In exile.
screen: `GOD HAD AN ADDRESS.` → `CAPTIVES BY THE RIVER CHEBAR.` → `THE HEAVENS WERE OPENED.`

segments.voice: What Ezekiel sees is hard to describe, and he knows it. A whirlwind comes out of the north, a great cloud, and fire folding in on itself, with a glow like bright metal at the center. Out of it come four living creatures, each with four faces: a man, a lion, an ox and an eagle. They have wings, and they move straight ahead without turning. Beside them are wheels, and the wheels are strange: they look, the text says, as it were a wheel in the middle of a wheel, and their rims are full of eyes. Wherever the spirit goes, the wheels go too. Above the creatures is a firmament like crystal, and above that, a throne, and on the throne a figure like a man, surrounded by brightness like a rainbow in the clouds. Listen to how careful the language is. Ezekiel almost never says this is what it was. He says the appearance of, the likeness of, as it were. When he reaches the top, he piles them up: "This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD." Three layers of distance before the name of God. Jewish tradition calls this vision the merkavah, the chariot. The Mishnah treats it with great caution: it is not to be taught even to one student, unless he is wise and already understands on his own. Mystics later built a whole path of contemplation around it. But the plain meaning is enough for today. The throne has wheels. The glory that seemed tied to one building shows up beside a river in a foreign land. The exiles are far from home, and Ezekiel's first chapter puts the vision of God's glory right there, beside them.
screen: `A STORM, FOUR LIVING CREATURES.` · `A WHEEL IN THE MIDDLE OF A WHEEL.` · then, large: `THE APPEARANCE OF THE LIKENESS OF THE GLORY.` · then: `THE THRONE HAS WHEELS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look up at something moving in the sky. If you can, go to a window or step outside. Find something in motion: a cloud, a bird, a plane, branches, even a ceiling fan if that's what you have. Settle, and breathe, and just watch it move. Don't name it or explain it. Let it be what it appears to be. Ezekiel was standing in an ordinary place, by a river in a foreign land, when the sky opened. Let the place where you are be ordinary, and still worth looking at. If you pray, you can pray from right where you are, the way the exiles had to. The bell holds the time.
Merkavah. The chariot: the name Jewish tradition gives to Ezekiel's vision of the throne with wheels, seen among exiles by the river Chebar. Today's word.
Your line: God in exile too. Today, when you're somewhere you'd rather not be, a waiting room, a commute, a hard meeting, look up once and take in where you are. Day eight hundred nine.

howItsDone: Jews read Ezekiel 1 as the opening of the book of Ezekiel, and in many communities it is chanted as the prophetic reading on the first day of Shavuot.

fork.setup: you're Ezekiel, a priest far from the Temple. the sky opens over a river in Babylon. how do you describe what you see?
options: say exactly what God looks like.
describe it as the appearance of a likeness.
fork.reveal: he describes it in careful layers: the appearance, the likeness, as it were. he writes it down without claiming to capture it.

original.note: Hebrew: chariot, the name tradition gives to Ezekiel's throne vision.

trapdoor: what you thought: Ezekiel saw a strange flying machine.
what it means: a vision of God's glory on a throne with wheels, seen in exile.
what a scholar hears: the merkavah, a text the Mishnah guarded and later mystics meditated on, written in layers of 'likeness'.

notes: The word 'merkavah' does not appear in Ezekiel 1; the script presents it as the name tradition gives the vision. Keeper may want to confirm framing.
Mishnah Chagigah 2:1 is paraphrased: the chariot is not expounded even to one, unless he is wise and understands on his own. Please check the 'single student' wording.
Ezekiel 1 as the haftarah for the first day of Shavuot appears only in howItsDone; Keeper please confirm.
'Mystics later built a whole path of contemplation around it' refers to merkavah/hekhalot mysticism; kept general by design.
The opening of Ezekiel 1:1 includes a date ('the thirtieth year'); the script leaves it out.

Editor: the text says 'river of Chebar', so 'canal' became 'river' throughout; the Mishnah Chagigah 2:1 paraphrase now says 'not even to one, unless he is wise' instead of 'only to a single student'; cut 'a Tuesday'.

Audit: the teach no longer says the chapter 'says God is there with them' (the text shows a vision, not that statement); 'the people of Judah' softened to 'many in Judah'; the garbled practice line ('not too far away') rewritten.
